a: Trying huge numbers of possible passwords until the right one is found
Tricking a user into revealing a password
Entering code into a text box
tasks.fb: No trickery: it's simply trial and error at high speed.

tasks.q: Which account is most at risk from brute force?
a: One with a short password made only of lower-case letters
One that locks after three failed attempts
tasks.fb: Fewer possible combinations means less time to crack.

tasks.q: How is a dictionary attack different from pure brute force?
a: It tries likely words and known passwords first, instead of every combination
tasks.fb: Most people choose predictable passwords, so this is much faster.

tasks.q: Why is reusing a password across sites dangerous?
a: If one site is breached, attackers try the same password everywhere else

tasks.q: Which password is hardest to brute-force?
tasks.fb: Length matters more than anything: a long passphrase has far more combinations.

tasks.q: Why does adding one character make such a difference?
a: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible combinations
tasks.fb: With 95 possible characters, each extra one multiplies the possibilities by 95.

tasks.q: Which of these belong in a strong password policy? Select all that apply.
opts: A minimum length of at least 12 characters
A mix of letters, numbers and symbols
A different password for each account
Writing passwords on a note by the screen
Using your name and year of birth
correct: A minimum length of at least 12 characters
A mix of letters, numbers and symbols
A different password for each account
tasks.fb: The last two make life easier for attackers, not for you.

tasks.q: Why do experts recommend a password manager?
a: It creates and remembers a different strong password for every site
It shares passwords with friends safely
It removes the need for any password
tasks.fb: You only have to remember one strong master password.

tasks.q: How does an account lockout stop brute force?
a: The attacker can only make a few guesses before the account is locked
tasks.fb: Millions of guesses per second becomes three guesses.

tasks.q: Why does two-factor authentication help even if a password is guessed?
a: The attacker also needs the second factor, such as a code on the user's phone
tasks.fb: Two-factor is one of the most effective defences there is.

tasks.q: What should a website store instead of your password?
tasks.fb: Hashing means even a stolen database doesn't reveal the passwords directly.

tasks.q: Why is hashing described as one-way?
a: You can turn a password into a hash, but you can't turn a hash back into the password
It only works on one computer
It can only be used once
It works only for short passwords
tasks.fb: Attackers have to guess, hash the guess and compare, which is slow if the password is strong.

tasks.q: Put these passwords in order, weakest first.
tasks.fb: Length beats complexity: a long passphrase is both stronger and easier to remember.

info.title: Billions per second
info.text: A powerful computer with graphics cards can test billions of password guesses per second against a stolen list of hashes.

info.title: The top password
info.text: Lists of leaked passwords are still topped by '123456'. It's usually the first guess an attacker makes.

info.title: Have I been pwned
info.text: Free services let you check whether your email address has appeared in a known data breach, so you know which passwords to change.

info.title: Three random words
info.text: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends three random words as a password: long, strong and easy to remember.

info.title: Rainbow tables
info.text: Attackers precompute huge tables of hashes to look up stolen ones instantly. Adding a random 'salt' to each password defeats this.

info.title: Not just logins
info.text: Wi-Fi passwords, phone PINs and even bike locks can be brute-forced. A four-digit PIN has only 10,000 combinations.
